ortho.holy_orders:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, ordination is one of the Holy Mysteries, in which a bishop lays hands on a man, and prays for the Holy Spirit to come upon him, ordaining him a bishop, priest or deacon. In Greek it is called cheirotonia, which means the laying on of hands.

The Orthodox understand that it is Christ who ordains through the bishop, and that the ordained minister serves the church, especially in the Divine Liturgy and other sacraments. Only men are ordained, and priests and deacons may be married if they marry before ordination, while bishops are usually celibate. A Protestant reader for whom ordination is an act by which a church recognizes a call should note that the Orthodox regard it as a sacramental act that conveys the grace of the Holy Spirit, in continuity with the apostles.
catholic.holy_spirit:
Catholics confess the Holy Spirit as the third person of the Holy Trinity, the Lord and giver of life, who is worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. In the Catholic understanding, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Gospel of John calls him the Paraclete, meaning the advocate or helper.

The Holy Spirit is understood to inspire the Scriptures, to guide the Church, to act in the sacraments, and to give gifts and holiness to the faithful. The Church emphasizes that the Spirit is at work through its structures and its sacraments. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and Protestants agree that the Holy Spirit is a divine person, and the main difference is in the way the Spirit is seen as working through the Church and its sacraments.
jehovahs_witnesses.holy_spirit:
Jehovah's Witnesses understand the holy spirit as God's active force, the power which Jehovah uses to carry out his purposes. It was used to create, to inspire the writers of the Bible, to guide and strengthen God's servants and to give them fruits such as love and joy. It is not a person, and it is not part of a Godhead.

Witnesses generally write holy spirit without capital letters, to show that they do not regard it as a person. They point to passages where the spirit is poured out, or where people are filled with it, and understand these as descriptions of a force rather than a being. A Protestant reader who confesses that the Holy Spirit is a divine person, equal to the Father and the Son, should note that Witnesses understand the same passages differently and do not accept the Trinity.
lds.holy_spirit:
Latter-day Saints believe in the Holy Ghost as the third member of the Godhead, a personage of spirit, who does not have a body of flesh and bone, as the Father and the Son do. They teach that the three are separate beings, united in purpose, rather than one being in three persons.

The Holy Ghost testifies of Christ and of truth, comforts, guides and sanctifies. After baptism, a person receives the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands, which they understand as the right to the constant companionship of the Spirit if the person remains worthy. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints use the name Holy Ghost, but understand the Godhead differently from the Trinity, and treat the gift as conferred by a priesthood ordinance.
oneness_pentecostal.holy_spirit:
Oneness Pentecostals speak of the Holy Ghost, or the Spirit of God, and understand it not as a third person distinct from the Father and the Son but as the one God himself in action, especially as he works in the human heart and dwells in the believer. God is spirit, and the Holy Ghost is the same God who is Father and who came in Jesus.

For this reason the coming of the Holy Ghost into a person's life is understood as God himself coming to live within. It is a central part of the Oneness understanding of salvation, and they expect it to be evident in a life of holiness and in speaking in tongues. A Protestant reader who confesses the Holy Spirit as a third person of the Trinity should note that Oneness Pentecostals honor the Spirit, but do not distinguish him as a separate person.
ortho.holy_spirit:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses the Holy Spirit as the third person of the Holy Trinity, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father alone. The Orthodox address the Spirit in a well-known prayer as the Heavenly King, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who is everywhere present and fills all things.

The Spirit is understood as active in creation, in the inspiration of the Scriptures, in the sacraments and in the lives of the saints. Every Orthodox Christian receives the seal of the Spirit in Chrismation, which is understood as a personal Pentecost. The goal of the Christian life is described as the acquisition of the Holy Spirit. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox teaching about the Spirit's person is close to their own, with a difference over the procession of the Spirit from the Father alone.
pentecostal.holy_spirit:
Pentecostals confess the Holy Spirit as the third person of the Trinity, fully God, and as a living presence who is active in the church and in the lives of believers today. The Spirit convicts of sin, brings new birth, dwells in every believer from conversion, and guides and empowers God's people for holy living and witness.

What marks Pentecostal teaching is the emphasis on knowing the Spirit by experience and not only by doctrine. Worship expects that the Holy Spirit will move among the congregation, healing, speaking and giving gifts as he wills. Pentecostals use both Holy Spirit and Holy Ghost. A Protestant reader from another tradition will find the doctrine of the Spirit's person familiar, but should note that Pentecostals give far more weight to the Spirit's present, experienced activity.
catholic.human_nature:
Catholics teach that human nature was created good, in the image of God, and that it has been wounded by original sin, but not destroyed. The wounds include ignorance, suffering, death and an inclination to sin, which is called concupiscence. Reason and freedom remain real, but they are not enough, without grace, to attain the supernatural end for which God made us.

Baptism removes original sin and gives new life, though the inclination to sin remains as a struggle. Grace does not replace nature but heals and elevates it. A Protestant reader from a tradition which speaks of fallen nature or total depravity should note that Catholics use the image of a wound and not of complete corruption, and hold that humans retain a real capacity for good and for knowing God, even though they need grace to reach him.
lds.human_nature:
Latter-day Saints teach that human beings are the spirit children of God, with the capacity to become like him. They also speak of the natural man, a phrase from the Book of Mormon, meaning the state of a person who yields to the desires of the flesh and is an enemy to God, until he yields to the Holy Spirit and becomes a saint through the Atonement of Christ.

They do not teach original sin. Their Articles of Faith say that people will be punished for their own sins and not for Adam's transgression, and they teach that children are born innocent. The Fall is seen as a necessary step, which made mortality, agency and growth possible. A Protestant reader who holds that human nature is fallen from birth should note that Latter-day Saints see human beings as inherently divine in origin and potential, though needing Christ to overcome the natural man.
ortho.human_nature:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that human beings are made in the image and likeness of God. The image is understood as the capacities that make persons rational, free and able to have communion with God, and the likeness as the goal toward which human beings are called to grow, by grace, which is called theosis.

The Fall damaged this nature and brought death and a tendency to sin, which the Orthodox call ancestral sin, but they do not teach that people inherit Adam's guilt, or that human nature is totally depraved. Christ took on human nature in the Incarnation in order to heal it. A Protestant reader who speaks of fallen nature should note that the Orthodox stress illness and death, instead of guilt, as the inheritance from Adam, and stress the goodness of human nature as created.
catholic.icons:
Catholics use sacred images, statues and icons in churches and homes, as reminders of Christ, Mary and the saints, and as aids to prayer. They teach that honor shown to an image passes to the person it represents. They carefully distinguish this veneration from adoration, which is due to God alone.

The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 defended the use of images, and the Catholic Church holds that, since the Son of God became visible in the Incarnation, it is right to represent him and his saints in pictures. Images are also understood to teach the faith to those who cannot read. Many Protestants are concerned about the commandment against graven images and about the danger of idolatry. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics do not worship images, and hold that they are aids to devotion and not objects of worship.
oriental_ortho.icons:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac churches, use icons in their worship and devotion. They are painted in styles of their own, such as the Coptic and Ethiopian traditions, and are venerated by kissing, lighting candles and bowing.

Like the Eastern Orthodox, they understand the honor given to an icon as passing to the person depicted, and not to the wood and paint, and they ground the use of images in the fact that God became visible in Christ. The Armenian tradition also honors carved stone crosses. A Protestant reader whose tradition avoids images in worship should note that these churches regard icons as a normal and important part of prayer, and treat them as windows to the holy, not as idols.
ortho.icons:
The Eastern Orthodox Church places icons at the heart of its worship and devotion. An icon is a painted image of Christ, Mary, the saints or a feast, made according to the church's tradition and often after prayer and fasting. Orthodox Christians kiss icons, light candles before them and bow, as a sign of honor.

They teach that this veneration is given to the person shown, and not to the material, and that it is different from the worship due to God alone. The use of icons is defended on the ground of the Incarnation: because the invisible God took a visible form in Christ, he can be depicted. The Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787 affirmed this. A Protestant reader who knows the commandment against making images should note that the Orthodox distinguish honor from worship, and regard icons as windows to heaven rather than as idols.
reformed.icons:
Reformed churches teach that God is to be worshiped only in the way that he has commanded in Scripture, and that the Second Commandment forbids making images to worship or to represent God in worship. For this reason, the Reformers removed statues and paintings from churches, and Reformed worship is centered on the Word, the sacraments and prayer.

They hold that God has given his own images for worship: the preaching of the Word and the sacraments. Reformed Christians do not oppose art in itself, and many value it in daily life, but they do not use images or icons in worship or as objects of veneration, and many object even to pictures of Christ. A Protestant reader from a Lutheran or Anglican church, where images and stained glass are common, should note that Reformed churches historically apply the principle much more strictly.
catholic.image_of_god:
Catholics teach that every human being is made in the image of God, as Genesis says, and that this gives each person an equal dignity from conception. The image is understood to consist mainly in the human capacity to know and love God, in reason and in free will, and in the spiritual soul that cannot be reduced to matter.

Sin damaged the image but did not destroy it, and Christ, who is the perfect image of the invisible God, restores it in believers. Catholic teaching draws on the image of God to explain why human life is sacred and why people are made for communion with God and one another. A Protestant reader who uses the Latin phrase imago Dei will find that Catholics use it in a similar way, with emphasis on dignity and on the capacity for relationship with God.
lds.image_of_god:
Latter-day Saints understand the statement that human beings are made in the image of God in a more literal way than most Protestants. They teach that God the Father has a glorified body of flesh and bone, and that human beings resemble him in body as well as in spirit. They also teach that each person is a spirit child of Heavenly Father, with a divine nature and potential.

This gives the phrase a family meaning: to be in God's image is to be his child, sharing his nature in embryo. Most Protestants understand the image of God as referring to human capacities such as reason, moral awareness and the ability to relate to God, and hold that God is spirit. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the language of the image of God, but build from it a teaching about human origin and destiny that Protestants do not accept.
ortho.image_of_god:
The Eastern Orthodox Church distinguishes between the image and the likeness of God, from the account in Genesis. The image is the capacity given to every person to know God, to be rational and free and to love. The likeness is the goal toward which humans are called to grow, by God's grace, in holiness and union with him, which the Orthodox call theosis.

The Fall obscured the image but did not destroy it, and Christ, who is the true image of God, restores it. The idea that human beings are icons of God shapes much of Orthodox thought about people and about the use of icons in worship. A Protestant reader who uses the Latin phrase imago Dei should note that Orthodox teaching adds the idea of growth into likeness, which makes the image the beginning and not the whole of the story.
catholic.immaculate_conception:
The Immaculate Conception is a Catholic teaching about Mary, and it is often confused with the virgin birth of Jesus. It refers to Mary's own conception. The Church teaches, in a dogma defined in 1854, that from the first moment of her existence Mary was preserved by God's grace from original sin, in view of the merits of her son Jesus Christ.

Catholics do not say that Mary did not need a savior. They teach that she was saved by Christ in a special way, by being preserved in advance rather than being cleansed afterwards. The teaching draws on the angel's greeting of her as full of grace, and on the church's tradition. The Church celebrates the feast on December 8. Most Protestants do not accept the teaching because they do not find it in Scripture, and Catholics see it as a truth rooted in tradition and in the church's understanding of Mary's role.
ortho.immaculate_conception:
The Eastern Orthodox Church honors Mary as the all-holy Mother of God, and it generally holds that she lived without personal sin, and it calls her Panagia, the all-holy one. It does not, however, accept the Roman Catholic dogma of the Immaculate Conception, as defined in 1854.

The Orthodox give two main reasons. The dogma was defined by the pope alone, and it rests on the Western understanding of original sin as an inherited guilt, which the Orthodox do not share, since they teach that people inherit mortality and a tendency to sin but not guilt. Orthodox writers differ about how to describe Mary's own holiness at her birth. Most Protestants do not accept the doctrine either, so a Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox reject it for different reasons from theirs.
catholic.incarnation:
Catholics confess that the eternal Son of God became man: the Word became flesh, as the Gospel of John says. He was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and was born as a real human being, while remaining truly God. The Church teaches that Christ is one divine person with two natures, divine and human, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.

The purpose of the Incarnation, the Church says, is for us and our salvation: to reconcile human beings to God, to show them God's love, and to be a model of holiness. Catholics honor Mary as the Mother of God because of it. A Protestant reader will find that the Catholic doctrine of the Incarnation is the same in substance as their own, with the difference in the honor paid to Mary.
christian_science.incarnation:
Christian Scientists distinguish between Jesus and the Christ. Jesus is the man who lived in Galilee and Judea, and Christ is the divine idea or message of God's love for humanity, which Jesus expressed more fully than anyone before or since. Jesus is honored as the Son of God and as the Way-shower, who showed by his life and works what spiritual truth can do.

Christian Science does not teach that God became flesh in the way many Christians describe the Incarnation. It emphasizes that Jesus revealed the true nature of God and of humanity as spiritual. A Protestant reader who confesses that Jesus is God incarnate, fully God and fully man, should note that Christian Scientists use the same names but understand the identity of Jesus and Christ, and the meaning of the incarnation, in a different way.
lds.incarnation:
Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ, who was the Son of God and Jehovah in the premortal life, was born into mortality as the son of Mary, the mother of his body, and of God the Father, who is the father of his physical body. They believe this was a real birth into a real mortal life, and call it the condescension of God.

They do not teach the Trinity, so they do not say that God became man in the sense of one being in three persons. They teach that Christ is a separate divine being from the Father, who took on a mortal body. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the language of the birth of the Son of God and of his coming in the flesh, but describe who he is and his relation to the Father in a way that differs from the traditional doctrine of the Incarnation.
oriental_ortho.incarnation:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, confess that God the Word became man for our salvation, born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit. They teach that in Christ divinity and humanity are united in one nature of God the Word incarnate, without confusion, mixture or change.

They emphasize the unity of Christ, so that all he did and suffered was the action of one and the same person, and they honor Mary as the Theotokos, the Mother of God. They have historically declined to use the Council of Chalcedon's language of two natures, though they teach that Christ is fully God and fully man. A Protestant reader should note that these churches agree with Protestants about who Christ is, and differ in the technical wording.
ortho.incarnation:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that the eternal Son of God became a human being, taking flesh from the Virgin Mary by the power of the Holy Spirit. He is one person with two natures, fully God and fully man, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon. The Orthodox sometimes speak of the enfleshment of the Word.

The Incarnation is central to Orthodox theology and worship. They teach that Christ took on human nature in order to heal and transform it, and a saying often attributed to Athanasius puts it that God became man so that man might become god, meaning that human beings are called to share in the divine life. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox teaching about who Christ is closely matches their own, but that the Orthodox give the Incarnation itself a saving role, alongside the cross and resurrection.
catholic.inerrancy:
The Catholic Church teaches that the books of Scripture are inspired by God and that they teach without error the truth which God wished to be put into the sacred writings for the sake of our salvation. This is stated in the Second Vatican Council's constitution on divine revelation.

This wording has led Catholic scholars to a range of views about what inerrancy covers. The Church has not required Catholics to hold that every detail of history or science in the Bible is precisely accurate in the modern sense, and it recognizes that the human authors used the literary forms of their times. It asks that Scripture be read in light of what the authors intended to affirm. A Protestant reader from an Evangelical background, which speaks of complete inerrancy, should note that the Catholic position places the emphasis on the saving truth of Scripture.
evangelical.inerrancy:
Many Evangelicals affirm the inerrancy of Scripture: that the Bible, in its original writing, is without error in everything it affirms, including matters of history and science, as well as in its teaching about faith and morals. A widely known statement of this view is the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy of 1978.

Some Evangelicals prefer to speak of the infallibility of Scripture, meaning that it does not fail to accomplish its purpose, and some limit the claim of inerrancy to matters of faith and practice. Evangelicals debate what inerrancy requires, but they generally treat the Bible as fully trustworthy because it is inspired by God. Other Protestant churches, particularly some mainline denominations, speak of the Bible's authority without the language of inerrancy, so a Protestant reader should note that this term is characteristic of Evangelicals.
ortho.inerrancy:
The Eastern Orthodox Church holds that the Holy Scriptures are inspired by the Holy Spirit and are true, but it does not usually frame the question in the terms of inerrancy, which grew out of modern Protestant debates. The Orthodox emphasize that the Bible is the church's book, written within the church and read within it, and that its truth is the truth of Christ.

The Orthodox tradition has often read Scripture in symbolic and spiritual senses as well as literally, and it does not treat difficulties in details as a threat to faith. The Fathers and the liturgy give the guide to reading. A Protestant reader accustomed to the vocabulary of infallibility and inerrancy should note that the Orthodox affirm the trustworthiness of Scripture, but their concern is to understand it within the life of the church, and not to defend it against modern challenges.
anabaptist.infant_baptism:
Anabaptists practice believer's baptism: baptism is given only to those who are old enough to make a personal confession of faith and to commit themselves to follow Christ and to the community of the church. The name Anabaptist, meaning rebaptizer, came from the early practice of baptizing adults who had been baptized as infants.

They do not consider infant baptism to be baptism in the biblical sense, since an infant cannot repent or believe. Children are understood to be safe in God's care and are taught the faith until they can make their own decision. A Protestant reader from a church that baptizes infants, such as a Lutheran, Reformed or Anglican church, should note that for Anabaptists baptism is both a sign of forgiveness and a public promise to live as a disciple and to be accountable to the congregation.
baptist.infant_baptism:
Baptists practice believer's baptism only, sometimes called credobaptism from the Latin word for I believe: baptism is given only to those who have personally professed faith in Christ. They do not find infant baptism in the New Testament, where baptism follows hearing the gospel and believing.

Baptist churches often hold a service of dedication for infants, in which parents commit to raising the child in the faith, but this is not baptism. A person who was baptized as an infant in another church is usually asked to be baptized as a believer on joining a Baptist church, and Baptists do not intend this as a judgment on that person's faith. A Protestant reader from a church that baptizes infants should note that the difference is about the meaning of baptism, not about respect for the family.
catholic.infant_baptism:
Catholics baptize infants, normally within the first weeks after birth. They teach that Baptism removes original sin and gives new life in Christ, and that God's grace does not depend on the child's understanding, but on his promise. The parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith.

The Church points to the accounts of whole households being baptized in the New Testament, and to the practice of the early church. It also teaches that children who die without Baptism are entrusted to God's mercy. Catholics understand that the baptized person will need to grow into the faith, and receive the other sacraments as he does. A Protestant reader from a Baptist or Anabaptist tradition should note that Catholics regard baptism as a gift from God and not as a personal profession, which is why it can be given to a child.
lutheran.infant_baptism:
Lutherans baptize infants, and teach that Baptism is God's action in which he washes away sin, gives new birth by the Holy Spirit and unites the child to Christ. It is not a human decision but a gift, and it is given to children on the ground of God's promise, which is meant for them as much as for adults.

Faith is understood as itself a gift of the Holy Spirit, which God can work in a child. The child is then taught the faith at home and in church as the baptized person grows. Lutherans consider a person's baptism to remain valid throughout life, and daily repentance a return to it. A Protestant reader from a Baptist tradition should note that Lutherans hold that baptism depends on God's promise and not on the person's understanding, so it can be given to infants.
ortho.infant_baptism:
The Eastern Orthodox Church baptizes infants, usually within the first weeks or months after birth. The child is immersed three times in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and is immediately chrismated and given Holy Communion. A godparent speaks the promises on the child's behalf.

The Orthodox understand this as the child's entrance into the life of the church, in which the child can receive God's grace before understanding it, and grow into the faith through prayer, the sacraments and teaching. They point to the New Testament accounts of whole households being baptized. A Protestant reader from a tradition that baptizes only believers should note that in Orthodoxy the baptism of an infant is complete initiation, including communion, and is not a preliminary rite.
reformed.infant_baptism:
Reformed churches baptize the infant children of believers. They teach that the sign of the covenant of grace, which in the Old Testament was circumcision, is now baptism, and that God's promises extend to believers and to their children, as the apostle Peter says in Acts. Baptism is therefore a sign and seal of God's promise, and of belonging to his people.

Reformed churches do not teach that baptism automatically regenerates a child. The promise must be received by faith, and parents promise to raise the child in the faith. This is sometimes called covenant baptism. Reformed churches also baptize adults who come to faith and have not been baptized. A Protestant reader from a Baptist church should note that Reformed Christians share the emphasis on faith, but see the covenant family, and not only the individual, as the setting for baptism.
catholic.inspiration:
Catholics teach that the books of the Bible were written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that God is their author, and that the human writers were also true authors who used their own abilities and style. The Church draws on the statement in the Second Letter to Timothy that all Scripture is God-breathed.

The Church holds that this applies to all seventy-three books of the Catholic canon, including the deuterocanonical books that Protestants often call the Apocrypha. Inspiration does not mean that the writers were merely taking dictation. Catholics say that the Bible must be read in the light of the whole, the living Tradition and the teaching of the Church. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and Protestants agree that Scripture is inspired, and differ about which books are included and how Scripture is interpreted.
lds.inspiration:
Latter-day Saints believe that the Bible is the word of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit. Their eighth Article of Faith states that they believe the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly. They mean that copying and translating over the centuries has left errors and omissions.

They also believe that the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price are inspired scripture, and that words spoken by prophets when they are moved upon by the Holy Ghost are scripture. Latter-day Saints in the English-speaking world generally use the King James Version. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the belief that the Bible is inspired, but do not hold that it is the only inspired book, and they treat its transmission with some reserve.
ortho.inspiration:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that the Holy Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit, who spoke through human authors. The words of Scripture are both the word of God and the words of men, and the Orthodox understand the authors as cooperating with the Spirit, not as passive instruments.

The Church has not defined a detailed theory of inspiration. It treats Scripture as the church's book, which was written in the church and is read in worship, and whose center is Christ, the Word of God. Its meaning is understood in the light of the Fathers and the liturgy. A Protestant reader who uses the phrases verbal inspiration or God-breathed will find that the Orthodox agree that Scripture is inspired, though they focus less on how inspiration works and more on how Scripture is received in the church.
churches_of_christ.instrumental_music:
Most Churches of Christ worship a cappella, meaning that the congregation sings without instruments. They point out that the New Testament commands and describes singing in worship but does not mention instruments in the assemblies of the early church, and that the church historically sang unaccompanied for centuries.

The conviction is that where Scripture is silent, the church should be careful not to add to what God has commanded. Worship is meant to be pure singing from the heart, with every voice taking part. Members generally do not regard people who use instruments as unbelievers, but consider unaccompanied singing to be the faithful pattern. A Protestant reader from a church with organs, guitars and bands should note that Churches of Christ treat the question as one of obedience to what Scripture authorizes, not as a matter of taste.
ortho.instrumental_music:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, worship has traditionally been sung without instruments. The Divine Liturgy is sung by a choir or by a chanter and the people, and the human voice is regarded as the proper instrument of prayer and praise. The music is chant, in styles that differ among Greek, Slavic and other Orthodox traditions.

Several reasons are given: that instruments were associated with pagan worship in the early church, that the voice carries the words of the prayers, and that the tradition is simply the way the church has always worshiped. It is a matter of tradition and custom, not doctrine, and some Orthodox parishes in the West use the organ. A Protestant reader from a church where organs, guitars and bands are common should note that in Orthodoxy the unaccompanied voice is the norm.
catholic.intercession_of_saints:
Catholics ask the saints in heaven, and especially the Virgin Mary, to pray for them, in the same way that they might ask a fellow Christian on earth to pray for them. They hold that death does not separate believers from the Church, and that those with Christ in heaven join their prayers with those still on earth. This is what the Catholic Church means by the communion of saints.

Catholics distinguish this carefully from worship, which is given to God alone. They teach that Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity, and that the saints' prayers do not replace his, but share in them. Many Protestants object that Christians should pray to God alone, and that Scripture does not show the dead being addressed. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics also pray directly to God, and understand asking a saint to pray as a form of fellowship, not a rival to Christ.
lds.intercession_of_saints:
Latter-day Saints do not pray to saints or to Mary. They teach that prayer is to be addressed to God the Father, in the name of Jesus Christ, and they see Christ as the one mediator. This is close to the Protestant position, and is a point on which Latter-day Saints differ from Catholic and Orthodox Christians.

They do honor the righteous dead, and believe that the spirits of the departed continue to live and to care about the work of God on earth, and some believe that they may assist the living. They also perform baptisms and other ordinances in temples on behalf of the dead. A Protestant reader will find that the phrase prayer only to the Father is familiar, but should note that Latter-day Saints have a broader understanding of the relationship between the living and the dead, based on their own scriptures and temple practice.
oriental_ortho.intercession_of_saints:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, ask the Virgin Mary, the martyrs and the saints to intercede for them. Their prayers and liturgies contain many petitions asking the saints to pray to Christ on behalf of the faithful, and the saints are commemorated on their feast days.

These churches understand the Church as one family, living and departed, united in Christ, so that asking a saint to pray is as natural as asking a friend. They teach that God alone is worshiped and that Christ alone is the Savior. Many Protestants find the practice troubling, on the ground that Scripture directs prayer to God. A Protestant reader should note that these churches see the saints' prayers as an expression of the communion of the whole church, and not as a substitute for prayer to God.
ortho.intercession_of_saints:
Eastern Orthodox Christians ask the saints, and above all the Mother of God, to pray for them. They believe that the saints are alive in Christ, and that they join in the prayers of the church. In the Orthodox understanding, this is the same kind of request as asking a fellow believer on earth for prayer, extended to the whole communion of the church.

Orthodox prayers sometimes use language that startles Protestants, for example, Most Holy Mother of God, save us. The Orthodox explain that God alone saves, and that they are asking for her help by her prayers to him. Orthodox worship is addressed to the Trinity alone. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox distinguish carefully between worship and veneration, and see the intercession of the saints as an expression of the unity of the living and the departed in the one Church.
adventist.intermediate_state:
Adventists teach that there is no conscious intermediate state between death and the resurrection. They hold that human beings do not have an immortal soul that lives apart from the body. At death a person rests, unconscious, in what the Bible calls sleep, until Christ returns and calls the dead from their graves.

They base this on passages such as the one in Ecclesiastes that says the dead know nothing. Adventists find comfort in the hope of resurrection, and they see it as the biblical answer to death. Many Protestants believe that believers at death are conscious and with the Lord, citing passages such as Paul's wish to depart and be with Christ, and use the phrase intermediate state for this. A Protestant reader should note that Adventists read the same passages as describing the moment of resurrection, which will seem immediate to the one who has died.
catholic.intermediate_state:
Catholics teach that at the moment of death each person undergoes a particular judgment, in which Christ decides their eternal destiny. The person goes either to heaven, immediately or after a purification in purgatory, or to hell. This is different from the general judgment, which will take place at the end of time when Christ returns and the dead are raised.

The Church does not teach that the soul sleeps. The souls of the just are with Christ, and the faithful on earth can pray for those undergoing purification. This differs from the Protestant idea of an intermediate state, in which the believer is with the Lord in an unspecified way awaiting the resurrection. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics give a more detailed account of what happens after death, with the possibility of purgatory, and treat the departed as remaining connected to the living.
lds.intermediate_state:
Latter-day Saints teach that at death the spirit separates from the body and enters the spirit world, where it awaits the resurrection. The spirit world is understood to have two parts: paradise, a state of rest and peace for the righteous, and spirit prison, for the wicked and for those who have not heard the gospel.

In the spirit world the gospel is taught to those who did not have the chance to hear it on earth, and they may accept it and repent. Living members perform baptisms and other temple ordinances on their behalf. All will be resurrected, and judged, after this period. A Protestant reader who thinks of an intermediate state as being with the Lord should note that Latter-day Saints describe a more active spirit world, with further opportunity to learn and to make choices before the final judgment.
ortho.intermediate_state:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that after death the soul experiences a particular judgment, and enters a state that anticipates its final destiny, while awaiting the general resurrection and the Last Judgment. The righteous have a foretaste of the joy of heaven, and those who reject God a foretaste of the pain of separation.

The word Hades is used for the realm of the dead. Orthodox teaching does not define the details, and there is a tradition of the soul's passage after death, sometimes called the toll houses, which some Orthodox accept and others do not. The Church prays for the departed, and believes that its prayers can help them. A Protestant reader who speaks of an intermediate state in which believers are with the Lord will find that the Orthodox agree that the dead live in God's care, while giving more room to prayer and mystery.
adventist.investigative_judgment:
Many Adventist bodies teach a pre-advent judgment: a judgment that takes place in heaven before Christ returns, distinct from the final judgment at the end of the age. It is usually connected with the prophecies of Daniel and with the Adventist movement's history in the 1840s, and it is often described as an examination of the records of all who have professed faith, showing whose faith is genuine.

Adventists who hold this teaching stress that it is meant as good news. Christ is the advocate and judge, and the judgment vindicates God's justice and those who trust in him. The most fully developed form of the teaching is found in the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and not every Adventist group holds it in the same form. A Protestant reader who expects one judgment at the end of the age should note that Adventists teach a judgment in stages, beginning before Christ's return.
seventh_day_adventist.investigative_judg:
Seventh-day Adventists teach that in 1844 Jesus began the second and final phase of his work as high priest in the heavenly sanctuary, which they call the investigative judgment. They base this on the prophecy in the book of Daniel about the cleansing of the sanctuary, and on the picture in the Letter to the Hebrews of Christ ministering in the true sanctuary in heaven.

In this judgment, they teach, the record of every person who has professed faith is reviewed, to show who has truly accepted Christ, before Christ returns. Adventists emphasize that Christ is the believer's advocate, and that the judgment is a sign of God's justice and of assurance for those in Christ. Many other Protestants do not accept this teaching, and some Adventists have also debated it. A Protestant reader should note that it is central to the Adventist understanding of history and of Christ's present work.
catholic.jesus_prayer:
The Jesus Prayer, in its usual form, is: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. It is a short prayer that comes from the tradition of the Christian East, and it is known to Catholics, especially those influenced by Eastern spirituality. The Catechism of the Catholic Church mentions it as a prayer that may be used.

Catholics may say the prayer repeatedly, in silence, as a way to keep the mind on Christ. It is not central to Catholic devotion, which more often uses the Rosary, the Liturgy of the Hours and other prayers. A Protestant reader who knows Jesus' teaching against vain repetition in prayer should note that Catholics who use the prayer regard it as a heartfelt appeal for mercy, with the name of Jesus at its center, and not as a mechanical formula.
oriental_ortho.jesus_prayer:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, know and use the Jesus Prayer, a short prayer asking the Lord Jesus Christ for mercy. It has deep roots in the monasticism of Egypt and Syria, where the early desert Christians used short repeated prayers to keep the mind fixed on God.

The prayer is used by monks and by lay people, sometimes together with a prayer rope. It expresses the same idea of praying without ceasing, and of calling on the name of Jesus with a humble heart. A Protestant reader who has heard that repeated prayers are vain repetitions should note that in these churches the words are not a formula to be recited without thought, but a means of quiet attention to Christ, and they see it as a form of the constant prayer commended in the New Testament.
ortho.jesus_prayer:
The Jesus Prayer is central to Eastern Orthodox spirituality. In its usual form it says: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. It is prayed silently and repeatedly, often with a knotted prayer rope, and sometimes together with the rhythm of the breath, as a way of praying without ceasing, as the apostle Paul commands.

The aim is prayer of the heart, in which the words gradually become part of a person's inner life, and the mind and heart are united in attention to God. This tradition is associated with monks known as hesychasts, but it is meant for all Christians. A Protestant reader who knows Jesus' warning against using many words in prayer should note that the Orthodox stress that the prayer is not magic or mechanical repetition, but a humble and honest cry to Christ, using his name.
catholic.justification:
Catholics teach that justification is both the forgiveness of sins and the inner renewal of the believer: God does not only declare a person righteous, but makes him righteous by pouring grace into his soul. It begins at Baptism, and it is a free gift, which no one can earn by works done before receiving it.

After that beginning, Catholics teach, a person cooperates with grace, and grows in justice through the sacraments, prayer and good works, which are themselves fruits of grace. Protestant teaching commonly says that justification is a declaration that a sinner is righteous, on account of Christ's righteousness counted as his, and that sanctification follows. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation issued a Joint Declaration agreeing on basic truths about justification, although differences of understanding remain.
lds.justification:
Latter-day Saints teach that justification comes through the Atonement of Jesus Christ. They understand it as being pronounced righteous, forgiven and accepted by God, and they hold that it takes place as a person receives the ordinances of the gospel, such as baptism, and keeps the covenants made with God, being sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise.

It is therefore not understood as a single moment in which a person is declared righteous by faith alone, but as an ongoing relationship that depends on continuing faithfulness. Latter-day Saints believe that Christ's grace and his merits make it possible, and that no one can be justified by his own works. A Protestant reader accustomed to the idea of a once-for-all declaration should note that Latter-day Saints describe justification in connection with covenants and obedience.
ortho.justification:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of justification, but does not treat it as a separate legal act distinct from a person's growth in holiness. Orthodox teaching understands salvation as a whole process of healing and being made righteous, in which forgiveness, sanctification and union with God are joined, and which is often described as theosis.

The Orthodox do not use the framework of a courtroom declaration as the main picture of salvation, and they are wary of separating being declared righteous from being made righteous. They teach that God's grace begins and enables the whole, and that people freely cooperate with it. A Protestant reader who knows justification as the central doctrine, and as a verdict of acquittal, should note that the Orthodox place it within a wider description of salvation as a journey of transformation in Christ.
reformed.justification:
Reformed churches teach justification by faith alone: God declares sinners righteous, not because of anything they have done, but because Christ's righteousness is credited to them, and their sins are counted against Christ. It is a legal or forensic declaration, a verdict of acquittal and acceptance, which is complete when a person believes.

Faith is not itself the ground of justification, but the instrument by which the sinner receives Christ. Justification cannot be separated from sanctification, the ongoing transformation of the believer's life, which follows as its fruit, though the two are distinct. Good works are the evidence of true faith, not its cause. A Protestant reader will find this the standard Protestant account, and Reformed churches consider it central and the doctrine on which the church stands or falls.
adventist.last_judgment:
Adventists teach that judgment takes place in stages. The first is the pre-advent judgment, which takes place in heaven before Christ returns, and which they understand as an examination of the records of those who have professed faith. Then, after Christ's return and the millennium, the final judgment takes place when the wicked are judged and destroyed.

Adventists stress that the judgment vindicates God's justice and that those who trust in Christ have an advocate. They also see the judgment as involving the saved in reviewing God's dealings, during the thousand years in heaven. A Protestant reader who expects a single Last Judgment at the end of time should note that Adventist teaching describes several phases, and places an important part of the process in heaven before the Second Coming.
catholic.last_judgment:
Catholics teach that at the end of time Christ will return in glory to judge the living and the dead. All the dead will be raised, and the secrets of all hearts will be revealed. The righteous will enter eternal life, and those who have refused God's love will go to eternal punishment. This is called the Last Judgment, or the general judgment.

It is distinct from the particular judgment which each person undergoes at the moment of death. The Church teaches that the Last Judgment will show the full extent of God's justice and mercy, and that it will be based on love shown to others, especially the poor, as Jesus described in the Gospel of Matthew. A Protestant reader will find the expectation of a final judgment shared, and should note that Catholics also teach an earlier judgment at death.
lds.last_judgment:
Latter-day Saints teach that after the resurrection, all people will stand before Jesus Christ to be judged according to their works, the desires of their hearts and their acceptance of the gospel. Christ is the judge, and his atonement makes mercy possible for those who repent.

The result of the judgment is not simply a division between saved and lost. Most people will be assigned to one of three kingdoms of glory, the celestial, terrestrial or telestial, according to how they lived and what they chose, and only a very few will be consigned to outer darkness. A Protestant reader who thinks of the final judgment as separating the saved from the condemned should note that Latter-day Saints describe a judgment with several outcomes, most of which are glorious.
ortho.last_judgment:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, that all will be raised, and that he will judge every person. The Last Judgment is remembered in the church's worship, in the icon of the Last Judgment often painted on the west wall of a church, and on a Sunday shortly before Lent that is devoted to it.

The Orthodox stress that the judgment reveals what each person has become, and how far he has loved God and his neighbor, and that Christ comes as both judge and lover of mankind. They pray for the departed, and hope for God's mercy at the judgment. A Protestant reader will find the belief in a final judgment familiar, and should note that Orthodox teaching pays special attention to love and to the revealing of the heart.
adventist.liturgical_calendar:
Adventists generally do not follow the traditional church year of Christian feasts and seasons in their worship, and many of them regard the seventh-day Sabbath as the principal holy time appointed by God. They are cautious about adding holy days that Scripture does not command, and historically have regarded some of them as human traditions.

Adventists differ in practice. Many members celebrate Christmas and Easter in family or community ways without treating them as sacred days, and some Adventist churches mark them with special services. Some Adventists are also interested in the biblical feasts of the Old Testament, though the church has not generally observed them. A Protestant reader from a church that keeps Advent, Lent and Easter should note that Adventist worship is centered on the weekly Sabbath rather than on the seasons of a liturgical year.
anglican.liturgical_calendar:
Anglicans keep the church year: Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, along with holy days that commemorate saints and other events. The year is structured by a lectionary which takes the congregation through much of the Bible over time.

The church year is understood as a way of walking through the life of Christ and of keeping the gospel central in the rhythm of worship. Anglicans also commemorate saints, though the degree of emphasis differs. Anglo-Catholics keep many feasts, and more Evangelical parishes may keep only the major seasons. A Protestant reader from a church that follows a program of its own each Sunday should note that in Anglican churches the readings and prayers follow a common calendar shared with many other churches.
catholic.liturgical_calendar:
The Catholic liturgical year is built around the celebration of the mystery of Christ. Its main seasons are Advent, Christmas, Lent, the Easter Triduum, Easter and Pentecost, along with Ordinary Time, and it is centered on Easter. Sunday Mass readings follow a three-year cycle so that a large part of Scripture is heard over time.

The calendar also includes feasts and memorials of Mary and of the saints on most days of the year, and certain holy days on which Catholics are obliged to attend Mass. Catholics understand the year as a way of living through the events of salvation and of sanctifying time. A Protestant reader who keeps Advent, Lent and Easter will find these familiar, and should note that the Catholic calendar also includes many days devoted to the saints.
ortho.liturgical_calendar:
The Eastern Orthodox liturgical year begins on September 1 and centers on Pascha, the Orthodox name for Easter. Twelve Great Feasts, including Christmas, Epiphany, the Transfiguration and the Dormition of Mary, mark the year, along with the seasons of fasting, and almost every day commemorates saints or events.

Some Orthodox churches use the older Julian calendar and others a revised version, so that Christmas falls on December 25 or on January 7 in the Western calendar. Pascha is calculated in a way that often differs from the Western date for Easter. The Orthodox regard the calendar as a way of living the mysteries of Christ in the rhythm of the year. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox calendar is more elaborate than most Protestant ones, and that the dates of feasts may not match those in the West.
anglican.liturgy:
Anglican worship is shaped by the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in the sixteenth century and revised many times, together with later prayer books in many provinces. Its services include daily Morning and Evening Prayer, and Holy Communion, and they are meant to be prayed together in the language of the people.

The idea of common prayer is that the whole church prays with one voice, using set forms so that Scripture, the Psalms and the creeds shape the faith of ordinary worshippers. Anglican worship ranges widely, from formal and ceremonial services to simpler and more informal ones, but the prayer book heritage usually gives it a shared structure. A Protestant reader from a church that plans its own order of worship each week should note that Anglican services follow a common text, and many Anglicans see the liturgy as teaching the faith as much as the sermon does.
catholic.liturgy:
The central act of Catholic worship is the Mass, which follows a set order in the Roman Rite, the most widely used form of Catholic liturgy. It has two main parts: the Liturgy of the Word, with readings from Scripture, a homily and prayers, and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, in which bread and wine are offered, consecrated and received in communion.

The prayers and structure of the Mass are fixed by the Church, and are the same in Catholic churches around the world, though now said in local languages, with the option of Latin. Catholics also pray the Liturgy of the Hours, the daily prayer of the Church. Other Catholic rites, such as the Byzantine rite of the Eastern Catholic churches, have their own liturgies. A Protestant reader who thinks of the sermon as the center of a service should note that in the Mass the Eucharist is the center.
lutheran.liturgy:
Lutherans understand the main Sunday service as the Divine Service, in which God serves his people by giving them his Word and sacrament, and the people respond with prayer, praise and thanksgiving. The service follows the historic pattern of the western church: confession and absolution, the Kyrie and hymn of praise, readings, the creed, the sermon, the prayers and the Lord's Supper.

Lutherans kept the liturgy at the Reformation, purified of what they considered unbiblical, because they regard it as a good way to teach and to carry the gospel. The degree of formality varies widely. Some congregations follow a full traditional liturgy, others use contemporary music and simplified forms, but most keep the core of Word and sacrament as the center of worship. A Protestant reader from a church without a fixed order of service should note that Lutherans value the liturgy as a way that God gives his gifts.
oriental_ortho.liturgy:
The central worship of the Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, is the Divine Liturgy, in which the Eucharist is celebrated. In the Syriac and Malankara traditions it is known as the Holy Qurbana, a word meaning offering. The liturgies are ancient, and use prayers, called anaphoras, that go back to the early centuries.

They are sung or chanted, often in the historic languages of the church, such as Coptic, Ge'ez or Syriac, alongside the local language, and they include incense, processions and much congregational participation. They can last two or three hours. The people receive Holy Communion in both kinds. A Protestant reader whose service is centered on preaching should note that in these churches the liturgy is understood as taking part in the worship of heaven, with the Eucharist at its heart.
ortho.liturgy:
The main service of the Eastern Orthodox Church is the Divine Liturgy, celebrated on Sundays and feast days, usually in the form attributed to John Chrysostom. It has two parts: the Liturgy of the Word, with hymns, litanies, the reading of the Epistle and Gospel and the sermon, and the Liturgy of the Faithful, in which the bread and wine are offered, consecrated and received in communion.

It is sung almost entirely, by a choir or chanter and the people, without instruments, and it includes icons, incense and candles. The congregation usually stands. It lasts an hour and a half or more. The Orthodox regard the liturgy as a participation in the worship of heaven, and the center of the life of the church. A Protestant reader accustomed to a service with a sermon at its center should note that the sermon is brief in the Divine Liturgy, and that communion is the center.
quaker.liturgy:
Many Friends practice waiting worship, also called silent meeting. The community gathers without a set order of service, a prepared sermon or a paid minister, and waits together in silence for the presence of God. Anyone who feels led by the Spirit may speak, briefly, and the others listen and hold the message in prayer.

The underlying conviction is that Christ teaches his people directly, so worship does not depend on a priest or a program. Not all Friends worship this way. Some Quaker meetings, particularly evangelical ones, have programmed worship with hymns, Scripture reading and a pastor's message. A Protestant reader accustomed to a service with hymns and a sermon should note that where worship is unprogrammed, the silence is not empty, but is understood as an active waiting on the Lord.
baptist.local_church:
Baptists understand the local church as a congregation of baptized believers who have covenanted together to worship, learn and serve, and who govern themselves under the headship of Christ. Each local church is autonomous, meaning that no bishop, denominational board or outside body can rule it.

Baptist churches join voluntarily in associations and conventions for mission, education and fellowship, but these do not have authority over the congregations. The members together call their pastor, receive new members and make decisions, in what is called congregational government. A Protestant reader from a church with a presbytery or a bishop should note that for Baptists the local congregation is the primary and complete expression of the church, and that wider bodies exist to serve it.
catholic.local_church:
In the Catholic Church, the local community of worship is the parish, a group of Catholics under the care of a pastor, who is usually a priest. Parishes are not independent. They belong to a diocese, which is led by a bishop, and through him are united with the pope and the whole Church.

In Catholic theology, the phrase local church usually refers to the diocese as a whole, since it is the bishop who represents the fullness of the church in that place. Catholics think of the universal Church as coming first, with parishes as the places where it is present in daily life. A Protestant reader who thinks of a local church as a self-governing congregation should note that a Catholic parish depends on the bishop and the wider Church, and does not make its own decisions about doctrine or leadership.
churches_of_christ.local_church:
In Churches of Christ, the local congregation is the whole of the church at that place, and it governs itself. There is no denominational headquarters, synod or governing body over the congregations. Each is led by a group of elders, sometimes called shepherds or overseers, who are chosen by the congregation, and served by deacons and often a preaching minister who is hired by the local church.

Congregations cooperate freely in mission work, in schools and in benevolent ministries, but these are voluntary arrangements and do not rule the churches. The conviction behind this is that the New Testament shows independent local churches led by their own elders. A Protestant reader from a denomination with a national body should note that Churches of Christ have no such body, and that practice can differ somewhat from one congregation to another.
catholic.magisterium:
The Magisterium is the Catholic Church's teaching authority, which belongs to the pope and to the bishops in communion with him. Catholics believe that Christ gave the apostles, and their successors, the responsibility to guard and to explain the gospel, and that the Holy Spirit guides them to do so faithfully.

The Church teaches that the Magisterium is not above the word of God, but serves it, by teaching only what has been handed on. In certain conditions, when the pope or the bishops together definitively teach a matter of faith or morals, their teaching is understood to be free from error, which is called infallibility. A Protestant reader who looks to Scripture alone should note that Catholics see the Magisterium as the authoritative interpreter of Scripture and Tradition together, so that questions of doctrine can be settled, and not left to each believer.
ortho.magisterium:
The Eastern Orthodox Church has no office comparable to the Catholic Magisterium. It holds that the truth of the faith is preserved by the whole Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, and is expressed through the bishops gathered in councils, the writings of the Fathers, the liturgy and the faith of the people. This is sometimes called the mind of the Church.

The consensus of the Fathers, meaning the agreement of the early church teachers, is treated as a guide, and the decisions of councils are confirmed when they are accepted by the whole church. Infallibility is not attributed to the pope or to any one bishop, but to the Church as a whole. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox agree with them in rejecting papal authority, but note that they place great weight on tradition and councils as the way the church holds the faith.
catholic.marks_of_the_church:
Catholics confess the four marks of the Church from the Nicene Creed: one, holy, catholic and apostolic. They understand the Church as one in faith, worship and government under the pope and the bishops, holy because Christ is holy and gives holiness through the sacraments, catholic in that it has the fullness of the faith and is meant for all people, and apostolic in being founded on the apostles and continuing their teaching and ministry.

Catholics believe that these marks are found fully in the Catholic Church. Protestants also say the Creed, but many follow the Reformers in identifying the true church by the right preaching of the Word and right administration of the sacraments. A Protestant reader will find the words familiar, and should note that Catholics give them a specific institutional meaning, including the succession of bishops and the unity of the pope.
ortho.marks_of_the_church:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses the four marks of the Church from the Nicene Creed: one, holy, catholic and apostolic, and believes that these are found in the Orthodox Church. It understands unity as unity in the one faith and the sacraments, holiness as belonging to Christ and to his Spirit, and apostolicity as the continuity of the apostles' teaching and ministry through the bishops.

The word catholic is understood as meaning according to the whole, that is, having the fullness of the faith, and this fullness is present in every local church gathered around its bishop, rather than in a universal jurisdiction. A Protestant reader who recites the Creed will find the marks familiar, and should note that the Orthodox understand catholic in a way that does not require a single head of the church on earth, like the pope.
catholic.marriage:
Catholics teach that marriage is a covenant between a man and a woman, by which they form a lifelong partnership ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children. When both are baptized, the marriage is a sacrament, a sign of the union between Christ and the Church, and it gives the couple grace.

The Church holds that a valid marriage is permanent, that it requires free consent, and that it should be open to children. In the Latin Church the couple themselves are understood to be the ministers of the sacrament, with a priest or deacon as the official witness. Marriages of non-baptized people are also valid, though not sacramental. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics regard marriage as a sacrament, and that this affects teaching on divorce and remarriage.
lds.marriage:
Latter-day Saints teach that marriage between a man and a woman is central to God's plan and that, when it is performed in a temple by proper authority, it can last beyond death and into eternity. This is called eternal marriage, or a sealing, and the couple's children can also be sealed to them.

They believe that families are meant to continue forever, and that being sealed is a requirement for the highest degree of glory. A civil marriage outside a temple is recognized as valid, but is understood as lasting only until death. In the nineteenth century some members practiced plural marriage, which the church ended in 1890. A Protestant reader whose tradition says that marriage ends at death should note that Latter-day Saints treat it as a covenant that can continue in the next life.
ortho.marriage:
The Eastern Orthodox Church regards marriage as a holy mystery, or sacrament, in which a man and a woman are joined before God, and are called to grow in love and holiness together. It is understood as an image of the union of Christ and the Church.

The distinctive feature of the marriage service is the crowning: the priest places crowns on the heads of the bride and groom, as signs of their sharing in the kingdom of God and of the sacrifice, even martyrdom, that love requires. They share a common cup, and are led in a procession around the table. Orthodox teaching holds that marriage is meant to be lifelong, though it allows remarriage in some circumstances. A Protestant reader should note that the service is not a legal contract but a sacramental blessing, in which God is understood to unite the couple.
catholic.mary:
Catholics honor Mary, the mother of Jesus, above all other saints. They call her the Blessed Virgin Mary, or Our Lady, and teach that she is truly the Mother of God, because her son is God, and that she remained a virgin, was conceived without original sin, and was taken up to heaven at the end of her life.

Catholics see Mary as the model of faith and obedience, and they ask for her prayers, in devotions such as the Rosary and the Hail Mary, which is built from words of Scripture. They distinguish the honor given to her from the worship that belongs to God alone. Protestants honor Mary as the mother of Jesus and as a woman of faith, but generally do not hold these later teachings or pray to her. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics regard devotion to Mary as leading to her son.
lds.mary:
Latter-day Saints honor Mary as the mother of Jesus, a virgin who was chosen and prepared by God to bring the Savior into the world. They teach that she conceived by the power of God, and they hold her in high esteem as a faithful and righteous woman and as an example of humility.

They do not pray to her or through her, and they do not teach the doctrines developed in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, such as the Immaculate Conception or her perpetual virginity. They do not usually call her the Mother of God, as their understanding of the Godhead differs. The Book of Mormon speaks of her as a virgin, most precious and chosen. A Protestant reader will find that Latter-day Saints treat Mary similarly to most Protestants: with honor, but without devotion.
oriental_ortho.mary:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, honor Mary as the Theotokos, the Mother of God, because the child she bore was God the Word made flesh. They teach that she remained a virgin, and they celebrate her Dormition, when she died and was taken up.

Devotion to Mary is very strong in these churches, with many feasts, hymns and prayers. The Coptic church holds that she has appeared in Egypt on several occasions, including in the twentieth century. They ask for her prayers as the greatest of the saints, while worship is reserved for God. A Protestant reader who honors Mary as the mother of Jesus should note that these churches give her a much larger place in worship, and that they understand this honor as protecting the truth about Christ.
ortho.mary:
The Eastern Orthodox Church honors Mary as the Theotokos, a Greek title meaning God-bearer, or Mother of God, and as the Panagia, the all-holy. They teach that she remained a virgin all her life, that she lived without personal sin, and that after her death she was taken up to be with her son.

The title Theotokos was affirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431 in order to protect the truth that Jesus is one person, both God and man. Mary is honored above all the saints and angels, and the Orthodox ask for her prayers, but they do not worship her. Many hymns, feasts and icons are devoted to her. A Protestant reader who honors Mary as the mother of Jesus should note that the Orthodox honor is greater, and that it is grounded in what they believe about Christ.
catholic.matrimony:
Catholics celebrate marriage as a sacrament in a rite in which the couple exchange their consent, in the presence of a priest or deacon, who witnesses in the Church's name, and at least two other witnesses. The rite is often celebrated within the Mass, and includes a nuptial blessing.

Catholics who marry are expected to do so according to the Church's form, and to prepare in advance, and a marriage of a Catholic outside this form is generally not recognized as valid without special permission. The marriage of a Catholic to a baptized non-Catholic is permitted with the approval of the Church. A Protestant reader accustomed to a wedding as a celebration in a church should note that Catholics regard it as a sacrament conferring grace and creating a lasting bond, and that the requirements of the Church apply.
lds.matrimony:
Latter-day Saints who wish to be married for eternity are married in a temple, in a ceremony called a sealing, performed by a priesthood holder with authority to seal. Only members who hold a temple recommend, a certificate of worthiness, may attend, so family and friends who are not members or who are not qualified cannot be present in the sealing room.

Many couples hold a wedding reception or a separate ceremony outside the temple, where everyone can be present. A civil marriage is also recognized, but does not include the eternal sealing. The ceremony includes covenants made between the couple and God. A Protestant reader accustomed to a wedding open to all guests in a church should note that in this tradition, the most sacred form of marriage takes place in a temple with restricted attendance.
ortho.matrimony:
The Eastern Orthodox marriage service, called the Mystery of Marriage, has two parts. The first is the betrothal, in which rings are blessed and exchanged. The second is the crowning, in which the priest places crowns on the couple's heads, in the presence of the congregation, praying that God will unite them and bless them.

The service includes readings about the wedding at Cana, a shared cup of wine, and a procession three times around the table with the Gospel book and cross. Orthodox teaching gives the priest's blessing an essential role in the sacrament. Marriage in the church is normally between two Orthodox Christians, though marriages with baptized non-Orthodox Christians are permitted under certain conditions. A Protestant reader should note that the service emphasizes the couple's share in Christ's kingdom, symbolized by the crowns.
catholic.means_of_grace:
Catholics teach that the seven sacraments are the principal means of grace, that is, the ordinary ways in which God gives his life to his people. They are Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Reconciliation, the Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony, and each was instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church.

The Church teaches that in the sacraments Christ himself acts, and that they give the grace they signify when they are validly celebrated and received with the right disposition. This is not automatic magic, since the person must be open to grace. Prayer, Scripture and works of mercy are also ways in which grace is received. A Protestant reader who knows the phrase means of grace as referring to the Word, prayer and the sacraments should note that Catholics use the same idea, and count seven sacraments where most Protestants count two.
lutheran.means_of_grace:
Lutherans teach that God gives forgiveness, life and faith through means: the gospel proclaimed in the Word and in the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Many also include absolution, the declaration of forgiveness. Through these ordinary, visible things the Holy Spirit works to create and to sustain faith.

Lutherans stress that these means are God's own actions and promises, and not human efforts to reach him. This is why Word and sacrament stand at the center of congregational life and why Lutherans look to them for assurance: the promise of forgiveness is spoken to you, and given to you in water, bread and wine. A Protestant reader who thinks of the sacraments as symbols should note that Lutherans hold that God really acts through these means, though they reject the idea that grace works automatically.
methodist.means_of_grace:
Methodists speak of the means of grace: the ordinary channels through which God gives his grace to his people. Following John Wesley, they name works of piety such as prayer, reading and hearing Scripture, the Lord's Supper, fasting and Christian fellowship, as well as works of mercy such as caring for the poor and the sick.

None of these earns salvation, but each is a place where God meets us and strengthens faith and love. Methodists stress that they should be practiced regularly and in community, and Wesley urged frequent participation in the Lord's Supper. The class meeting, small groups for mutual accountability and encouragement, was another means that gave early Methodism its character. A Protestant reader will find that Methodists understand the phrase broadly, to include acts of mercy and Christian fellowship as well as sacraments.
reformed.means_of_grace:
Reformed Christians speak of the means of grace: the ordinary ways God uses to give and strengthen faith. The Westminster Shorter Catechism names the Word, the sacraments and prayer as the outward means by which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption.

The preaching of the Word is central. The two sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, are signs and seals of the promises of the gospel. These means work not by any power in themselves but through the Holy Spirit, and by faith. They are the ordinary channels, though God is free to work in other ways. A Protestant reader will find this familiar, and should note that Reformed churches emphasize regular attendance at the worship of the church, where the means are used together.
adventist.millennium:
Adventists teach that the thousand years of the book of Revelation take place in heaven, after the Second Coming of Christ. At his return, the righteous dead are raised and the righteous living are taken to heaven, while the wicked die, and the earth is left desolate, in a condition in which Satan is bound to it for the thousand years.

During this period the saved take part in reviewing God's judgments. At the end, the holy city, the New Jerusalem, descends to earth, the wicked are raised and judged, and they are destroyed, and God makes a new earth. Adventists do not expect an earthly reign of Christ before this, and do not teach a secret rapture. A Protestant reader accustomed to premillennial or amillennial views should note that the Adventist millennium happens in heaven and not on earth.
catholic.millennium:
The Catholic Church has no dogma that Christ will reign on earth for a literal thousand years. It has been cautious about millenarianism, the expectation of an earthly kingdom before the end, and it teaches that the final victory of Christ will come through the last judgment, and not through a historic triumph of the Church.

Many Catholic teachers, following Augustine, read the thousand years in the book of Revelation as symbolic, describing the period of the Church between Christ's first and second coming, in which Satan's power is limited. This is close to what Protestants call amillennialism. The Church does not require any one interpretation. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics generally do not expect a future earthly millennium, and place their hope in the return of Christ and the resurrection.
evangelical.millennium:
Evangelicals hold a range of views about the thousand years mentioned in the book of Revelation. Premillennialists teach that Christ will return before the thousand years and reign on earth, and some, called dispensationalists, link this with a particular scheme of biblical prophecy. Amillennialists read the thousand years symbolically, as the present age between Christ's first and second coming.

Postmillennialists teach that the gospel will bring a golden age before Christ returns. All Evangelicals hold that Christ will return personally and visibly, and that there will be a final judgment and a new creation. They may differ on the details without regarding them as a test of faith. A Protestant reader should note that Evangelicals have no single position on the millennium, though premillennialism is common in popular teaching and in many Baptist and independent churches.
jehovahs_witnesses.millennium:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Christ's thousand-year reign, described in the book of Revelation, is still to come in its fullness and will follow the destruction of the present wicked system at Armageddon. During it the earth will be turned into a paradise, the dead will be resurrected and humans will be gradually raised to perfection.

They believe that Christ began to rule as King in heaven in 1914, and that his presence is invisible, with the events of the last days now taking place. At the end of the thousand years there will be a final test, and those who rebel will be destroyed. A Protestant reader should note that Witnesses share the language of a thousand-year reign, but connect it with their own teaching about 1914, an earthly paradise and the resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous.
lds.millennium:
