Latter-day Saints teach that the Second Coming of Christ will begin a thousand years of peace, called the Millennium, in which Christ will reign personally on the earth. Satan will be bound, the earth will be renewed, and the righteous who have died will be resurrected at the start and live with Christ.

During the Millennium, they teach, temple work for the dead will continue, and people who are still living in mortality will be taught the gospel. At the end there will be a final test, and then the final judgment. Latter-day Saints also expect that the New Jerusalem will be built in the Americas, and that Jerusalem in the Holy Land will also serve as a center. A Protestant reader who knows premillennial views will find similarities, and should note the emphasis on temple work.
baptist.mode_of_baptism:
Baptists baptize by immersion: the person is fully placed under the water and raised up again. They point out that the Greek word for baptize means to immerse, and that the New Testament accounts describe people going down into the water. It is understood as a picture of burial and resurrection with Christ, as the Letter to the Romans says.

Baptist churches usually have a baptistery, a pool built into the sanctuary, or use a river or lake. Baptists do not accept sprinkling or pouring as baptism, though they generally do not doubt the sincere faith of those who were baptized in that way. A Protestant reader from a church that baptizes by pouring or sprinkling should note that Baptists treat the mode as important because it is bound up with what baptism symbolizes.
catholic.mode_of_baptism:
Catholics baptize with water, and the Church accepts either immersion or pouring water over the head as valid, as long as the person is baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the Western church, pouring has been the usual practice for many centuries, and immersion is also permitted.

In many Eastern Catholic churches immersion is the usual practice. In an emergency, any person, even a non-Christian, may baptize with water and the proper words, if he intends to do what the Church does. What matters, according to Catholic teaching, is the water and the Trinitarian words. A Protestant reader from a Baptist tradition, which insists on immersion, should note that Catholics regard pouring as fully valid, though they recognize immersion as a fuller sign of burial with Christ.
oneness_pentecostal.mode_of_baptism:
Oneness Pentecostals baptize by immersion: the whole person is placed under the water, in the name of Jesus Christ. They understand this as picturing burial and resurrection with Christ, as taught in the Letter to the Romans, and they follow the pattern they see in the New Testament.

Baptism is given to those who repent and believe, and infants are not baptized. Sprinkling or pouring is not regarded as baptism. Members who were baptized in another way, or by another formula, are generally asked to be baptized again in Jesus' name when they join. A Protestant reader from a Baptist church, which also baptizes by immersion, should note that the difference lies in the formula, the name of Jesus, and in the understanding of baptism as part of the new birth.
ortho.mode_of_baptism:
The Eastern Orthodox Church baptizes by triple immersion. The priest, or the godparent, holds the person, usually an infant, and immerses the person three times in the water, once for each person of the Trinity, saying the words of baptism. The three immersions are also understood to recall Christ's three days in the tomb.

Full immersion is the normal practice, and pouring is allowed only in cases of necessity, such as illness. Baptism is followed at once by chrismation, and by Holy Communion. The Orthodox regard the mode as part of the ancient tradition of the church, and as a strong sign of dying and rising with Christ. A Protestant reader who knows Baptist immersion of adult believers will find a similar mode, applied to infants and adults alike, and repeated three times.
community_of_christ.mormon_label:
Members of Community of Christ generally do not call themselves Mormons. The church was known until 2001 as the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, or RLDS, and traces its history to those who did not follow Brigham Young to Utah but reorganized under the leadership of Joseph Smith III.

It understands itself as a Christian church within the Restoration tradition that began with Joseph Smith, but it is a separate body with its own name, its own governance and different practices. Many members are uncomfortable when others use the term Mormon for them, since in common speech it usually means the church headquartered in Salt Lake City. A Protestant reader should note that Community of Christ and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are different churches, and that members appreciate being called by the church's present name.
